content: Cervical cancer is the second most prevalent cancer among women under the age of 65 and is the leading cause of death from gynecological cancers globally. The lifetime risk of developing cervical cancer by the age of 65 is approximately 0.69% in developed countries and 1.38% in developing countries. Although Pap smear screening enables early detection of cervical cancer at a potentially curable stage, a significant number of women still present with advanced or metastatic disease, which is associated with a poor prognosis. The integration of platinum-based chemotherapy with radiotherapy has demonstrated improved outcomes compared to radiotherapy alone. However, 30% to 50% of patients either fail to respond to treatment or experience disease recurrence. For these patients, there are no universally accepted standard treatment options, although platinum-based chemotherapy is commonly employed, and clinical trials are ongoing to explore alternatives. The primary objective of this study was to compare various types and combinations of cytotoxic chemotherapy for the treatment of metastatic or recurrent cervical cancer. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to January 2012. They also reviewed reference lists from relevant studies and review articles. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving chemotherapy for metastatic or recurrent cervical cancer were included. Trials that involved radiotherapy, chemoradiotherapy, intra-arterial chemotherapy, biological agents, or immunomodulators were excluded. Three independent reviewers assessed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the risk of bias. The analysis revealed that there were no available data comparing best supportive care with chemotherapy. Cisplatin-based chemotherapy regimens were the most commonly studied and widely used. Some non-platinum chemotherapy regimens demonstrated response rates comparable to cisplatin-based regimens, but they were associated with higher toxicity. The most frequently used cisplatin regimen involved a dose of 50 mg/m² administered on day 1 of a 21-day cycle. Higher doses of cisplatin did not result in improved survival outcomes. There was no direct comparison between single-agent cisplatin and carboplatin in the available data. Overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were inadequately reported across the studies, and quality of life (QoL) outcomes were insufficiently documented. Combination chemotherapy regimens involving cisplatin were found to be more toxic than single-agent regimens. However, the limited data available suggested that this increased toxicity did not significantly worsen quality of life. No significant differences in response rates were observed based on the site of recurrence, although there was a trend toward improved response rates when the primary site of disease was located outside the previously irradiated pelvic region. The authors concluded that combination cisplatin-based chemotherapy may be a viable treatment option for patients with good performance status who have recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer. However, the response rates and survival improvements associated with these regimens remain modest, and the associated toxicity is significant. Outcomes for these patients are generally poor, underscoring the need for further research into novel cytotoxic and biological agents, as well as optimal treatment scheduling. Future clinical trials should aim to provide more comprehensive survival and quality of life data and should include planned subgroup analyses based on prior treatments and the site of recurrence.
